prompt.context: You are sitting in one of Chicago's oldest scotch bars with a fellow intern. It is a Friday night after a busy week at your summer internship. The weather is mild—a perfect summer evening. While enjoying one of the bar's finest stogies and sipping an 18-year old McCallen single malt, your friend asks you how much you think the bar is worth.
prompt.question: Using a back-of-the-envelope calculation, how would you go about determining the value of this bar?

clarifying_info.a: The bar sells two things: liquor and cigars. The average cost of a cigar is $9 and the average cost of a drink is $12.

clarifying_info.q: What is the bar's maximum capacity?

clarifying_info.a: The bar is located on one of Chicago's busier streets for foot traffic.
The bar is open Tuesday through Sunday from 5 pm until 2 am.

clarifying_info.q: How many staff does the bar have?
clarifying_info.a: A bartender, a waiter, and a waitress. All three were there the entire evening.

clarifying_info.q: What discount rate should I use?
clarifying_info.a: The discount rate typically used for bars of this genre is 13%.

clarifying_info.q: What is the annual growth rate of cash flows?
clarifying_info.a: The bar's cash flow is growing at 3%—the rate of inflation.

exhibits.title: Daily Sales
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down daily sales figures by time period (Fridays & Saturdays vs. Rest of Week) and season (Spring/Summer vs. Fall/Winter), with a base daily sales figure and seasonal adjustment factors.

framework: Estimate annual revenues using customer volume and average spend, segmented by day type and season
Estimate annual costs: separate fixed costs from variable (COGS) costs
Calculate EBIT = Revenue - Variable Costs - Fixed Costs
Apply tax rate to get after-tax cash flow (NOPAT)
Apply perpetuity growth formula: Value = CF / (r - g) to arrive at present value

questions.guidance: Candidate should build revenue from daily sales figures, distinguishing between Fridays/Saturdays (busier) and the rest of the week (Tue-Thu + Sun = 4 days), and between Spring/Summer (25 weeks) and Fall/Winter (25 weeks). A strong candidate drives this segmentation proactively before receiving Exhibit 1. After the approach is outlined, hand Exhibit 1. Revenue should total $568,000.

math.setup: Break revenue into 4 buckets: Fri/Sat in Spring-Summer, Rest-of-Week in Spring-Summer, Fri/Sat in Fall-Winter, Rest-of-Week in Fall-Winter. Year = 50 weeks (25 Spring-Summer + 25 Fall-Winter). Bar closed Monday, so Rest-of-Week = 4 days (Tue-Thu + Sun).

questions.prompt: What are the bar's annual costs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm fixed costs (rent, maintenance, management, insurance, liquor license, employees) and variable costs (cost of goods sold). After brainstorming, reveal: variable costs = 20% of total revenues; fixed costs = $120,000.

math.setup: Variable costs = 20% of revenues; Fixed costs = $120,000

questions.prompt: What is the after-tax cash flow of the bar?
questions.guidance: Candidate subtracts total costs from revenues to get pre-tax income, then applies the 40% tax rate to arrive at after-tax cash flow.

math.setup: Pre-tax income = Revenue - Total Costs; After-tax CF = Pre-tax income × (1 - tax rate)

questions.prompt: How do you perform a valuation of the business?
questions.guidance: A great candidate recognizes the need to discount a stream of future cash flows. Use the growing perpetuity formula: Value = CF / (r - g). Discount rate = 13%, growth rate = 3%, so r - g = 10%. Numerator is the after-tax annual cash flow of ~$200,000.

math.setup: Growing perpetuity: Value = CF / (r - g). CF = $200,000, r = 13%, g = 3%.

questions.prompt: What might drive variation in these revenue numbers?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify two main drivers: (1) day of the week — Fridays and Saturdays are typically busier than other days; (2) seasonality — people tend to be out more during summer than winter.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the possible fixed costs and variable costs for this bar?

categories.name: Variable Costs
ideas: Cost of goods sold (liquor and cigars — approximately 20% of revenues)

recommendation: Based on a back-of-the-envelope DCF, the bar is worth approximately $2 million
This is derived from estimated after-tax annual cash flows of ~$200,000 discounted at a net rate of 10% (13% discount rate minus 3% growth rate) using a growing perpetuity formula
risks: Revenue estimates are sensitive to assumed occupancy rates and seasonal adjustments
Fixed cost base could be higher than assumed (e.g., rent in a high-foot-traffic Chicago location)
Liquor license renewal and regulatory risk
Key-person risk if business depends on specific staff or reputation
next_steps: Obtain actual financial statements to validate revenue and cost assumptions
Benchmark against comparable bar transactions in Chicago
Assess lease terms and renewal risk
Verify liquor license status and any pending regulatory changes
